translation:
Questions on stealing from the guru: 1 — of the acrobat (vadi); 2 — of the barber (khavas); 3 — of Naradji.

Second question — Shri Jivandasji said that once an acrobat (vadi) went out to display his skills. There he saw a lake in a great forest. Being thirsty, he sat down to drink water, and there he saw a crane catch a fish in its beak. The crane first caught the fish by the tail and tossed it high up; it tossed it in such a way that, turning it around, it caught it again by the head, in its mouth. The acrobat saw this. Then it occurred to his mind: 'I already know many skills, but this skill is new — let me master it and profit from it.' So he set about mastering the skill. He first practiced the whole technique with the bow and then with the spear. Having mastered the arrow, he then practiced the throw called jhang — catching the spear in his teeth and hurling it, then catching it again by turning and gripping it by the haft. Performing this feat, he played at many royal courts and grew infatuated with fame.

Once, before a certain king, another acrobat was performing, and this acrobat went and joined the contest. A rivalry arose between them, and the newly arrived performer began to show the feat he had newly learned. The very first time, the feat came off perfectly and he was overjoyed, and the other acrobat lost; the king, the ministers, and all the people were astonished. Then the defeated acrobat and the others asked where he had learned this feat, and he answered that he had learned it by his own wit — concealing his guru. At this the leader of the defeated acrobat said, 'There can be no skill without a guru — he has stolen [hidden] his guru. Make him perform again; this time he will not get away with it. If he wins a second time, we will accept it as proven' — so they told the king. So he was made to perform a second time, and this time he forgot the trick's timing. Because of that, the spear went from above straight into his mouth and passed clean through, piercing his whole body and going into the ground.

On this, Jivandasji said that because he stole [betrayed] the duty he owed his guru, he lost his own life — he gained a bad name in this world, and in the world beyond he was left belonging to neither side.

_Vigahamki vidya lai, bakhar barchhi jhil. Rajab guru gun chaurte, mukh mein paithi shil. ||1||_ (Having learned the art from the crane bird, [the acrobat] could catch the flung spear — but Rajab says: by hiding the debt owed to his guru, the spear went into his mouth.) The acrobat, having learned the skill from the crane, used to catch the thrown spear (sang) with the skill he had gained; but Rajabji says that by concealing the favor of his guru — the crane — the spear went into his mouth.

The second question is of King Bhoj. He knew all the fourteen sciences existing in the three worlds, but he was thinking of learning a fifteenth science, when at that time a sannyasi (renunciant) arrived. The king served and entertained him greatly, and as he was leaving, the sannyasi said, 'King Bhoj, tell me whatever wish is in your mind — you speak to me with such earnest requests that it seems you have a desire, so speak it.' Hearing this, the king submitted his request: teach him the fifteenth science, that of entering another's body (parkaya pravesh). The sannyasi said, 'Come to the cremation ground at night, and bring materials for the fire-offering (homa).'

As the king was about to go alone, Queen Bhanumati said, 'Take the barber (khavas) with you — do not go alone.' So the king set off, taking the barber along. He told the barber, 'You sit here,' and himself went on to the sannyasi's hermitage to learn. But the barber secretly followed and, hidden in the king's shadow near the hermitage, began to learn as well — without either the king or the sannyasi knowing, he stole the teaching for himself. Afterward the king came back to where he had left the barber, and the barber returned to his spot too. Both then performed the fire-offering and practiced the mantra, each on his own.

Now the thought arose in the barber's mind: when the king tested the power, he would enter the king's body and enjoy Bhoj's kingdom himself. Holding this thought, he went along with the king. On one occasion, to test the power, the king killed a deer and told the barber, 'Watch over my body.' The king then entered the deer, and at that the barber entered the king's body. The king, now in the deer, thought, 'The barber will kill me now,' and fled in the deer's form. The barber then had his own original body cremated, and, in the form of Bhoj, went to Bhanumati's palace.

When the queen offered him a pot of water, the king would always recite a particular verse at that moment — but this one, not reciting the verse, hurried straight into the palace. At that the queen understood that though the body was the king's, the spirit within it was a barber's. Resolving to punish him for this, she said, 'My lord, I am keeping a vow, so do not come to my chambers for six months.' Hearing this, he turned back and went instead to the house of the queen who was out of favor.

Now the barber thought: since the king was in the form of a deer, he should have that deer killed. So he ordered his attendants, 'Let us go hunting today.' They went to the forest, where the king was among a herd of deer; they surrounded the herd, recognized the king, and shot an arrow at him, so that the king fled with a lamed leg. He then told his attendants, 'Bring me the particular deer I have in mind, from among those that fled' — giving them the sign that it was the lame one — and they went on to kill many deer.

King Bhoj realized they meant to kill him; at that moment he left the deer's body — there lay in a thicket the body of a dead parrot — and made his soul enter that parrot, abandoning the deer's body. Then, in the form of a parrot, he came to the queen and, speaking in a human voice, told her everything, saying, 'You sent the barber with me, and because of that I have suffered terribly — he has stolen my art of entering another's body.' Hearing this, the queen consoled him, saying, 'I will get your own body restored to you; do not worry at all.' Comforting the king in this way, she kept him, in the form of a parrot, in a cage, and cared for him with great affection.

At that time, seeing among the deer killed by arrows one that must have been the king, and believing the king had perished, the barber came to Bhanumati. Seeing that the queen daily cared for the parrot in the cage and showed it the greatest, most loving regard, it occurred to that fellow's mind: 'She loves this parrot more than she loves me — if I enter this parrot's body with my soul, the queen's affection for me will grow.' Thinking so, he set about beguiling the queen in every way he could. Then the queen said, 'You have learned the art of entering another's body — teach it to me, and demonstrate it, so my mind may be satisfied; without that, I remain displeased with you.'

Hearing this, the barber, pleased, said, 'One can enter a dead body, but not a living one — so let a corpse be brought, and I will demonstrate it to you.' At that moment, looking out from a window, the queen saw at a distance the corpse of a dog that had just died in great agony; she had that corpse brought and said to the barber, 'First enter this dog's corpse with your soul and show me — only then will you teach me the art.' At the queen's word, the barber left the king's body and entered the dog's corpse. At that, King Bhoj, lord of men, made his soul pass from the parrot's body back into his own original body, and everyone then beat that dog severely and drove it away.

On this the Vaishnav Jivandasji said that one who turns against his true benefactor has no place even in the three worlds.

(This matter of entering another's body is also found in the Prabandh Chintamani, Canto 1; Nazar no. 1, page 99.)

Once Vikram heard that without the art of entering another's body, even the powers of the yogi Bhairavanand were incomplete. To obtain that art he went to Shri Parvat and stayed near a yogi named Bhairavanand, serving that yogi for a long time. Before Vikram's arrival, a certain Brahmin had already been serving that same yogi in order to obtain this art, but up to then the Brahmin had not received it. This Brahmin said to Vikramaditya, 'You must not abandon me and take the art of entering another's body from the guru for yourself alone' — thus the disciple pressed him insistently. So the king began to petition the guru, who was preparing to give him the art, saying, 'First give the art to this Brahmin, then give it to me.' The yogi said, 'O King, this Brahmin is not fit for the art of entering another's body — he is utterly unfit,' and went on to say, 'If I give it to him, you will regret it.' Yet, because of the king's insistence, the guru gave the Brahmin the art as well.

Then both, having received the art from the guru, came to Ujjain. To test the art, seeing that the palace's finest elephant had died and the royal household was grieving over it, the king, in order to experience the art of entering another's body, entered the dead elephant's body himself.

Vikram already knew that once his own body lay empty, this Brahmin might enter it and take his kingdom; yet, since he was one devoted to relieving others' suffering, he took this risk without regard for his own body. Just as Vikram had suspected, the Brahmin did enter the king's abandoned body and began to rule the kingdom with a show of righteousness. The Brahmin also began to make use of Vikram's queen, so that an intimate bond formed between the two of them. One day a pet parrot that the queen loved dearly suddenly died. Vikram, in the elephant, thought: 'The queen's body has become the Brahmin's to enjoy; my chance of her touch is gone. Well, here is a good opportunity — if I enter the parrot's body, I will at least have the touch of the queen's gentle hands.'

Thinking so, the king entered the dead parrot's body, and the dead parrot suddenly came alive; because of this the queen's affection, which she had already had for the parrot, grew even greater. The Brahmin, who had become deeply infatuated with the queen, was constantly devising ways to please her, and he came to see that the queen loved the parrot even more than she loved him. So he thought, 'If the chance comes, I myself will become the parrot.' Vikram, residing in the parrot's body, discerned this plan. He was watching for a chance to leave the parrot's body, and just then he saw the empty shell of a dead lizard. Vikram quickly left the parrot and entered the lizard's body; seeing this, the Brahmin left the king's body and at once slipped into the parrot. The king then left the lizard's body and swiftly returned to his own original body. The unfortunate Brahmin, through his own deceit, in trying to gain the kingdom and the queen, lost his own body and, become a parrot, ended up shut in a cage. The queen and the king, having learned the whole matter from the king himself, treated that parrot with great harshness. In this way the accomplishment of the art of entering another's body came to pass.

Regarding entering another's body, Shankaracharya too made use of this art. When he defeated Mandan Mishra in philosophical debate, Mandan Mishra's wife said that he had won only half the victory, since a wife is the 'other half' of her husband — the printed text leaves the quotation itself blank at this point, giving only an empty pair of quotation marks — and so he would have to defeat her as well to be counted a complete victor; and she, as Saraswati, then put to him a question about the art of love.

_Prichchhami vad kamasya kala bhihato kimatmika. Kiyatyashcha kimadharastatha kamasya ka sthitih. Purvapakshe pare naryam nare tishthati va katham. Eteshamuttaram dehi savichary yatishvar._ (O lord of ascetics, what is the true nature of the arts of love, and how many are there, and on what do they rest? How does desire abide in human beings? In the bright and the dark halves of the month, where do these arts of love reside in man and in woman? Answer these questions after due reflection.) 'O lord of ascetics, what is the nature of these arts of love? And how many are there? And on what do they depend? In what manner does desire abide in human beings? In the bright fortnight and the dark fortnight, where do the arts of love reside in man and in woman? Please answer these questions after careful thought.'

Shankaracharya thought: if he did not answer, it would be a blot on his omniscience; if he did answer, it would be a blot on his vow of renunciation. So he asked for a month's time, and — there being a King Amarak who had died from the strain of hunting — in order to gain full experience of the amorous ways of that king's beautiful queens, he entered the dead king's body, and composed there an excellent treatise full of ever-fresh subjects on the science of love, which is today famous under the name Amarushatak.

In the Bhagavat, Canto Eleven, Chapter Fifteen, verses 23 and 24, it is said regarding entering another's body:

_Parkayam vishansiddha, atmanam tatra bhavayet. Pindam hitva vishetprano, vayubhutah shadandhrivat. ||23||_ _Pashnyarpidashcha gudam pranam, hriduh kanthanmurdhasu. Arohya brahmarandhrena, brahma nitvotsrijettanum. ||24||_ (A siddha wishing to enter another's body first contemplates the self within that body; then, leaving the gross frame behind, the life-breath, become as air, slips out effortlessly, as through six doors. To leave one's own body: pressing the anus with the heel, and raising the breath-conditioned self, that is, the subtle body, step by step through the heart, chest, throat and head, and carrying it out by the mind through the crown aperture, one abandons the gross body.)

When one wishes to enter another's body, the yogi first contemplates his own self within that body. Then he leaves his gross body behind and, carrying the subtle body (linga sharir) with him, enters effortlessly, just as a bee passes from one flower to another without labor; in the same way, by the path of the vital air, he enters the other body with ease. This accomplishment is called 'entering another's body' (parkaya praveshan). (23)

The method of leaving one's own body is then given: pressing the anus firmly with the heel of the foot, and raising the self conditioned by the vital breath — that is, the subtle body — step by step through the heart, chest, throat and head, and, through the door that is the crown aperture (brahmarandhra), carrying it by the mind into the other body, one abandons one's own gross body. This is reckoned the accomplishment called entering another's body. And when one draws the breath-conditioned self entirely out from one's own body through the door of the crown aperture without entering another body, that is reckoned the accomplishment called 'death at will.' (24)

Note — Bhagat Mohanbhai Motibhai of Tandalja tells me that a man of a lower-caste community in his village knew how to turn from a man into a tiger. When asked how this was done, that man said this is not an art anyone should wish to learn: when the change from man to tiger takes place, a tiger's tail emerges, and at that moment there is very great pain. This man used to take the form of a tiger in order to go to Amadra to meet his beloved. Dated 1 May 2006 — as of today, this bhagat, now 103 years old, is still living.

Giving the example of the acrobat, Jivandasji said that one who turns against his true benefactor has no place even in the three worlds.

Third question — Narad, son of Brahma, in his first incarnation was the son of a maidservant, and he lived in the town of Purajit. There the eight Vasudevs once came, and he served them with great devotion; because of this worthiness he came to be called Narad. Kripanath [the Lord] commanded this Narad, 'O Narad, go and take a guru, then come back.' Narad said, 'Whom shall I make my guru?' Then Kripanath commanded, 'Go to the town of Purajit; setting your own judgment aside, take a guru there — take initiation from whoever you meet first.'

Narad came and stood at the gate of the town of Purajit. A fisherman, going with a net over his shoulder to catch fish, came by. Narad fell at his feet and said, 'My lord, I take refuge in you.' The fisherman, pleased in turn, gave him initiation and said, 'When you fall into great suffering, remember me.'

Narad then came to Vaikunth. Countless devotees, Brahma, Rudra, and other gods were present there. The Sanakadi sages said, 'O Narad, whose teaching have you brought — name your guru.' Narad thought that 'fisherman' was too lowly a name to speak. At that Kripanath said, 'O Narad, go and undergo the eighty-four lakh births, and then return.'

Narad, weeping and lamenting bitterly, made his way back toward Purajit. Just then the fisherman, having caught his fish, was returning to his own home. He met Narad and found him lamenting, and asked, 'Who has caused you this suffering?' Narad said, 'My lord, when I spoke your name my heart did not feel glad — because of that I am being made to undergo the eighty-four lakh births.' The fisherman, growing angry, said, 'Who has the power to send my own disciple into the eighty-four lakh births?' Then he said, 'Tell Kripanath to set the eighty-four lakh forms before me, that I may pass through them all at once and be done. When Kripanath sets forth those forms, you go around them in circumambulation, prostrating upon them; and when Vasudev speaks, say: I undergo the eighty-four lakh births before your very eyes.'

Kripanath then came, called Narad, and embraced him, granting him the boon: 'I cannot manage even for a moment without you.' Regarding Naradji, Kabirji says:

_Guru duraya apna, to parharya kartar._ (When one keeps one's guru at a distance, the Creator abandons him.) When Narad kept his guru hidden and at a distance, God abandoned Narad.

_Kabir Narad haripad paiya, dhimarke updesh. Chaurasi fera mitya, bohor na kado bhes._ (Through the fisherman's teaching Narad attained the abode of God; the cycle of eighty-four lakh births came to an end, and he needed take no further birth.) Das Kabirji says that through the teaching of the fisherman, Naradji attained the abode of God, and the round of eighty-four lakh births came to an end for him, so that he never had to take another birth.

_Kabir Narad sarikha shishya hai, guru hvai machhimar. Ta guruki ninda kare, padai chaurasi dhar._ (Even if the disciple is as excellent as Narad and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, whoever reviles such a guru must fall into the eighty-four lakh forms of life.) Das Kabirji says that even if the disciple be of a lineage as excellent as Narad's, and the guru of a lineage as humble as a fisherman's, still, whoever reviles such a guru must fall into the eighty-four lakh wombs.

Just as Naradji received no honor in Vaikunth without a guru, the same happened to Shukdev; here is the couplet (sakhi) on that:

_Kabir garabh yogeshar guru bina, lage harki sev. Kahe Kabir Vaikunthate, fer diya Shukdev._ (Shukdev, a great master-yogi from birth, took up devotion to God without a guru — yet God sent him back out of Vaikunth.) Das Kabirji says that Shukdev, who was a great master-yogi (yogeshvar) from birth itself, began devotion to God without taking a guru; yet, without a guru, all his practice came to nothing, because God sent him back out of Vaikunth.

_Kabir Janak Videhi guru kiya, laga harki sev. Kahe Kabir Vaikunthme, ulati mila Shukdev._ (He then took Janak Videhi as guru and served with devotion, and this was accepted by the Lord; afterward Shukdev reached the abode of God.) Das Kabirji says that Shukdev then took Janak Videhi as his guru and performed devoted service, and this became acceptable to the Lord; afterward, having grown detached from worldly life, Shukdev reached the abode of God.

_Kabir Shukdev sarikha feriya, to ko pave par. Guru bin nigura jo rahai, padai chaurasi dhar._ (If even Shukdev was turned back for want of a guru, who without one can cross this world? The guruless must fall into the eighty-four lakh births.) Das Kabirji says that when even Shukdev, a master-yogi from the very womb, was pushed back into the world of the eighty-four lakh births for want of a guru, then who without a guru can hope to cross over worldly existence? So those without a guru will surely have to fall into the stream of the eighty-four lakh births.

_Lakhya mite nahi Jivana, je kachhu lakhiya lekh. Sadguru lekh mitaiya, tab paya aap alekh. ||2||_ (Whatever is written as fate cannot be erased — yet the true guru erased that writing, and then the unknowable Name was attained.) Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, whatever record of deeds destiny has written cannot be erased by anyone — but the true guru (sadguru) erased that writing of fate, and then we came to that Name of God which cannot otherwise be known.

_Likhita Chitraguptena lalatakshara-malika. Tanna chalayitu shakya asurais-tridashairapi. Na sapi chalitum shakya panditaih tridashairapi._ It is said in another Purana: the garland of letters that Chitragupta has written on the forehead cannot be moved even by gods, demons, pandits, or Shiva himself.

_Yaddhatra likhitam bhale tanmrisha naiva jayate. Rite Shri Ramdasanam prem nirbhar chetasam._ (What the Creator has written on the forehead never proves false — except for the true servants of Ram, whose hearts overflow with love.) Whatever the Creator has written on the forehead never turns out false — but this rule holds for everyone except the supremely loving servants of Ram, whose hearts are full of love.

_Kabir jo lakh supai alekhaku, adrishta akshar bij. To lakh rahe alekhaki, lakhu mite hi ghij._ (If we fix our aim on the God who cannot be shown, the seed of the unseeable arises in us, and that God's regard then rests on us; trust that the writing of fate will surely be erased.) Das Kabirji says that if we surrender our aim toward that God who can be shown by no one, a seed is sown from which that unseeable God arises within us; then such an unseeable God's regard rests upon us, and you may trust with certainty that whatever is written by past deeds will surely be erased.

_Alakh lakhayo Jivana, Sadguru Sitaram. Karma dharma vede kahyo, so chhand diyo bekam. ||3||_ (The sadguru made known the unseeable Lord, Sitaram; the rites the Vedas prescribed we abandoned as useless.) Maharaj Jivandasji says: O Jivan, the sadguru made known to us the unseeable Lord, the hidden Supreme Being who is Sitaram; and the ritual practices — japa, austerity, and the various rites the Vedas' karma-kanda prescribes — we have abandoned those useless labors.

_Kabir shishya hoy Narad sarikha, guru hoy machhimar. Tad guruku parhare, to vako var na par. ||4||_ (Even if the disciple be as high as Narad and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, if such a guru is abandoned no good comes of it.) Das Kabirji says that even if the disciple is of as high a standing as Narad, and the guru as lowly as a fisherman, still, if such a guru is abandoned, no good comes of it for the disciple at all.

_Kabir hem garam gau vipra ghan, e to paap aghor. E bache guru bandagi, par guru drohi nahi thor. ||5||_ (Stealing gold, or killing a cow or a Brahmin, are terrible sins — one is saved by taking refuge in the guru, but there is no refuge for one who betrays the guru.) Das Kabirji says that stealing gold, killing a cow, or slaying a Brahmin are extremely terrible sins; yet one is saved from them by taking refuge in the guru — but for one who betrays the guru, there is no refuge at all.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahi thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaur, jagatman jakadai marto. Samje na kem nathor, sajjan vachan uchaarta. Trikam kahe chhe takor, samjan hoy to samaj sadya. E to paap aghor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ Das Kabirji says that stealing gold, or killing a cow or a Brahmin, is a terrible sin, but one is saved by taking refuge in the guru — yet for the betrayer of the guru there is no refuge. One can never be saved from betraying the guru, and such people become entangled in worldly bondage; O shameless one, why do you not understand? Good people have spoken these very words. Trikamdas draws attention to this teaching: if you have the sense to understand, understand it quickly — to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a terrible sin.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahin thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaur, kahe chhe Kabir pokari. Samjat nahi nathor, jivan bhar rahe bhikhari. Samjan sadguru aur, guru karine samaj sadya. E to paap adhor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ To steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a terrible sin, but one is saved by taking refuge in the guru — yet for the one who betrays the guru there is no escape at all. Kabirji cries out and declares that one can never be saved from betraying the guru, but the shameless, brazen person understands nothing, and so is ruined for his whole life; the sadguru has given us this excellent understanding, so make haste to understand it by taking a guru — to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is indeed a great sin.

_Hem harn gau vipra vadh, e to paap aghor. Te chhute guru bandagi, guru drohi nahin thaur._ _Guru drohi nahi thaure, santo kahe pokari. Samjo nahi matimand, tethi fare bhikhari. Nugarane narakman thaur, sajjan shabdne samjo sadya. E to paap adhor, hem haran gau vipra vadh._ The fool does not understand, and so wanders about helpless, like a beggar. Those without a guru must fall into hell — so, virtuous brothers, understand these words quickly: to steal gold, or to kill a cow or a Brahmin, is a great sin.

_Kabir hari ruthe gati ek hai, je guru sharanagat jay. Par guru rithe gati ekau nahi, hari nav deve thay. ||6||_ (If God is displeased, taking refuge in the guru can save one — but if the guru is displeased, God will not grant shelter.) Das Kabirji says that if God is displeased, there is one remedy: going to the refuge of the guru, by which one may be saved; but if the guru is displeased, then God will grant that person no shelter at all.

_Hari ruthe hat ek chhe, guru sharanagat jay. Guru ruthe gat ko nahi, sant shastra sahu gay._ _Sant shastra sahu gay, guru droh gambhir ganay. Rau rau narak pahay, Ramayan path bhanay. Trikam sadguru kahay, guru drohi bahu dukh sahe. Guru sharanagat jay, hari ruthe gat ek hai._ If God is displeased, one is saved by taking refuge in the guru; but if the guru is displeased, there is no escape at all — so say the scriptures of the saints, [by which even God cannot save such a person]. The scriptures of the saints say that offense against the guru is reckoned a grave sin, and one must fall into the raurava hell — this is told in the account of Kag Bhushundi in the Ramayana. Trikam says that the true guru Kabir himself has spoken this: one who betrays the guru must endure much suffering, but if it is God who is displeased, then there is this one remedy — that one is saved by taking refuge in the guru.

_Kabir guru mahila guru bavaya, guru devan ka dev. Jo tu chelu kharo shayano, to karle guru ki seva. ||7||_ (Even a guru who seems mad or bewildered is still the god of gods — a wise disciple serves the guru all the same.) Das Kabirji says that even if the guru seems mad, deranged, or utterly bewildered, still the guru is the greatest, the very god of the gods; so if you are truly a wise disciple, render service and care to the guru.

_Kabir guruke avagun ankho dekhe, so to hove andh. Chhot kare parsadki, so kude bhav sindhu._ (Whoever looks with his own eyes for the guru's faults becomes blind; whoever spurns the guru's grace as untouchable drowns in the ocean of worldly existence.) Das Kabirji says that whoever looks with his eyes for the guru's faults becomes blind, and whoever treats the guru's grace as untouchable drowns and dies in the waters of the ocean of worldly existence.
